answers.text: Power can be shared among governments at different levels. There is a general government for the entire country and governments at the provincial or regional level. In India we call them the Central or Union Government and the State Governments. The constitution clearly lays down the powers of the different levels of government, so power is divided between higher and lower levels. This is called federal division of power, and it is also called vertical division of power.

Vertical division of power means power is divided between higher and lower levels of government. One government is for the whole country and others are for the provinces or regions. Not all countries have provincial or state governments, but India does. The same idea goes below the state level to the municipality and the panchayat.

In our country there is one government sitting in Delhi that looks after the whole nation, and every state like Kerala or Punjab has its own government too. Our constitution writes down exactly what each of them is allowed to do, and that is why power is split between the top level and the lower levels. Even villages have their own panchayat and towns have a municipality.

Power is not all with one government. The national government handles things for everyone in the country, while the government of each state handles things for that state, and the rule book of the country, the constitution, fixes which level does what. Because of that fixed list, power is shared from the top level down to the lower levels.

Think of it like a school: the principal runs the whole school and class teachers run their own classes. In the same way India has a Union government for the whole country and State governments for each state, each with its own powers given by the constitution.
Power is shared between the Central Government and the State Governments.
There are governments at different levels. One is for the whole country and others are for regions.
Vertical division of power means power is divided between the legislature, the executive and the judiciary. Each level checks the others.
Every country in the world has state governments under the central government, and the constitution lays down what each level can do. Power is divided between higher and lower levels.

There are two routes. In coming together federations, independent States come together on their own and pool their sovereignty to form a bigger unit, so the States usually have equal power, like the USA, Switzerland and Australia. In holding together federations, a large country decides to divide its power between the States and the national government, so the central government tends to be more powerful, as in India, Spain and Belgium.

In holding together federations a large country divides its power between the constituent States and the national government. Here the central government is usually more powerful than the States. India is an example of this.

Some countries are made when separate independent countries decide by themselves to join and become one big country, and since they joined as equals, each of them keeps equal strength. America is like this. Others start as one big country that later hands out some of its power to its states, so the centre stays stronger; India and Spain are like this.

In the USA the states were already independent and agreed to unite for security, so they all have similar power. In India the whole country chose to give some powers to the states, which is why the central government has more say.
Coming together is when free states merge by choice and share power equally. Holding together is when one big nation splits its power among its parts.
Federations can be coming together or holding together. USA is coming together and India is holding together.
In coming together federations, independent states join on their own to form a bigger unit.
India is a coming together federation because the states came together to form the country. In coming together federations the states have equal power.
India became a federation when independent states like Kerala and Punjab joined on their own, so India is a coming together federation like the USA.

Communalism was seen as a major challenge to democracy, so the makers of our Constitution chose the model of a secular state. There is no official religion for the Indian state, and the Constitution does not give a special status to any religion. It gives all individuals the freedom to profess, practice and propagate any religion, or not to follow any, and it prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion.

The Constitution allows the state to intervene in the matters of religion to ensure equality within religious communities, for example it bans untouchability. But a secular Constitution alone is not sufficient; communal prejudices have to be countered in everyday life and religion-based mobilisation in politics.

India does not have a state religion, unlike Pakistan which has Islam. Every person can follow, preach or practise whatever religion they like, or no religion at all, and nobody can be treated unfairly by the government because of their religion.
Because fighting between religious groups could break our democracy, the people who wrote the Constitution decided India would not belong to any one religion.

The government can step into religious matters if it is needed to make people equal inside a religion, like when it made untouchability illegal. Still, just having good laws is not enough; we also have to fight prejudice in our daily lives.
India is a secular state.
In India there is no official religion.
A secular state means the government has nothing to do with religion at all, so it can never interfere in any religious matter.
Secular means the state stays completely away from religion. India has no official religion and people are free to follow any religion.

For comparing countries, income is considered one of the most important attributes, because more income means more of all things people need. Total income is not useful for comparison since countries have different populations, so we use average income, which is the total income of the country divided by its total population. It is also called per capita income.
The World Bank's World Development Report uses per capita income to classify countries into high income or rich countries and low-income countries. India comes in the low middle income countries.

If you just add up all the money a country earns, a country with lots of people will look rich even if each person is poor. So we divide the country's total earnings by the number of people living there and compare that number instead.
Average income is what you get when you take a nation's whole income and share it equally among everyone who lives there.

Countries are compared mostly by income because having more money is thought to mean people can get more of what they need. The World Bank puts countries into rich and poor groups using income per person, and India is in the lower middle group.
Per capita income is used to compare countries.
India is a low middle income country according to the World Bank.
The country with the biggest total income is the most developed, so we just compare total income of countries.
China earns more in total than any other country, so it must be the most developed. Per capita income is total income divided by population.

There are more people in agriculture than necessary, so even if a few people move out, production will not be affected. Such workers are underemployed: they apparently work but all of them work less than their potential, and this hidden underemployment is called disguised unemployment.

Laxmi's family of five works on a small plot of land and everyone is working, but no one is fully employed. In cities, casual workers like painters, plumbers and repair persons also face underemployment.

On many farms there are too many hands for the work. If two brothers left to work in a factory, the farm would still produce just as much, which shows they were not really needed there. Everyone looks busy, but each person is doing less than they could, so this unemployment stays hidden.
A plumber in a city might get work only a few days a week and earn very little even though he is working.
Five people working on a field that needs only three look employed, but their real work potential is wasted. It is unemployment you cannot see.
Disguised unemployment is a type of unemployment in agriculture.
There are more people working in agriculture than needed.
Disguised unemployment means people are lazy and do not want to work, so they sit idle.
In disguised unemployment workers refuse to work hard, which is why farm output is low. If some leave, production falls.

In a barter system, both parties have to agree to sell and buy each other's commodities. This is called double coincidence of wants. Money acts as an intermediate in the exchange process, so it eliminates the need for double coincidence of wants. That is why money is called a medium of exchange.
Money acts as an intermediate in exchange and is called a medium of exchange.

A shoe maker who wants wheat has to find a farmer who has wheat and also wants shoes. Both must want what the other has. With money, the shoe maker sells shoes to anyone for money and then buys wheat from anyone, so he no longer needs that exact match. Money sits in the middle of every trade.
Without money you would have to find someone who wants your thing and has the thing you want at the same time, which is very hard.
Money works like a bridge between buying and selling, so you don't need to find a person who wants exactly what you have.
Money is used to buy things.
Double coincidence of wants is a problem in barter.
Money is useful only because the notes and coins are valuable in themselves, like gold.
We use money because it is precious in itself. In barter both people must want each other's goods.

Alluvial soil covers the entire northern plains. It was deposited by the Indus, the Ganga and the Brahmaputra, and it is also found in the deltas of the Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri. Alluvial soils are very fertile and contain potash, phosphoric acid and lime, which are ideal for sugarcane, paddy and wheat. Due to its high fertility, these regions are intensively cultivated and densely populated.

According to age, alluvial soil is old alluvial called Bangar and new alluvial called Khadar. Bangar has more kanker nodules, while Khadar has more fine particles and is more fertile. The soil is made of sand, silt and clay.

The rivers coming from the Himalayas, the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra, dropped this soil across the whole of north India, and you also find it where rivers like the Godavari and Krishna meet the sea on the east coast. It is so good for farming that lots of people live and grow crops there.
The newer river soil, Khadar, is finer and richer than the older Bangar soil, which has lumps of kanker in it.
This soil is very rich because it has potash, phosphoric acid and lime, so crops like rice, wheat and sugarcane grow very well in it.
Alluvial soil is found in north India.
Alluvial soil is very fertile.
Bangar is more fertile than Khadar because it is older and has more kanker.
Old alluvial soil, Bangar, is the most fertile, and new Khadar soil is less fertile. Alluvial soil is found in the northern plains made by the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra.

The denudation of the soil cover and subsequent washing down is described as soil erosion. Soil formation and erosion usually balance each other, but human activities like deforestation, over-grazing, construction and mining disturb this balance, and that leads to gullies and bad land.

Running water cuts through clayey soils and makes deep channels called gullies. The land becomes unfit for cultivation and is called bad land; in the Chambal basin such lands are called ravines. Sometimes water flows as a sheet over large areas down a slope and washes away the top soil; this is sheet erosion. Wind also blows loose soil off flat or sloping land.

Soil erosion is when the top layer of soil is stripped off and carried away. Normally new soil forms as fast as it is lost, but when people cut forests, let animals overgraze, build or mine, that balance breaks and the land gets cut into deep channels.

When rain water rushes down it digs deep cuts in the ground, and the land becomes useless for farming, like the ravines of Chambal. Other times a thin layer of water flows over a whole slope and slowly takes away the top soil.
If a farmer ploughs straight up and down a hill, the furrows act like little canals and the water rushes down fast, carrying the soil away.
Soil erosion is caused by wind and water.
Soil erosion means washing away of soil.
Gully erosion and sheet erosion are the same thing; both are just water taking soil away.
Sheet erosion is the same as gully erosion because both make deep channels in the soil.

Joint forest management is a programme that involves local communities in the management and restoration of degraded forests. It has been in formal existence since 1988, when Odisha passed the first resolution for it.

JFM depends on local village institutions that protect degraded forest land managed by the forest department. In return, the members of these communities get non-timber forest produce and a share in the timber harvested by successful protection.

In JFM the villagers living near a damaged forest form a committee and guard it along with the forest department. Because they protect it, they are allowed to collect things like fruits and leaves from the forest and they also get part of the wood when trees are cut.
The idea is that people from nearby villages help bring a damaged forest back to life together with the government.
Odisha was the first state to start it, in 1988. Village groups look after the forest and in exchange get to use forest produce other than timber and some of the timber.
JFM is about forests.
Joint forest management started in Odisha.
Under joint forest management only the forest department protects the forest and the villagers get nothing from it.
In JFM the government guards the forests alone; local people are not given any share of the timber or produce.
Tankas are underground tanks in Rajasthan used to store rainwater.

Regulating and damming of rivers affects their natural flow, causing poor sediment flow and excessive sedimentation at the bottom of the reservoir. This results in rockier stream beds and poorer habitats for aquatic life. Dams also fragment rivers, making it difficult for aquatic fauna to migrate for spawning. Ironically, the dams built to control floods have triggered floods due to sedimentation in the reservoir.

Multi-purpose projects induced earthquakes and caused water-borne diseases and pests. Irrigation changed the cropping pattern, with farmers shifting to water intensive and commercial crops, which led to salinisation of the soil. They also cause inter-state disputes like the Krishna-Godavari dispute, and large scale displacement of people.

When a river is blocked, the mud it normally carries piles up behind the dam instead of moving downstream, so the riverbed below becomes stony and fish lose their homes. Because the reservoir fills up with this mud, it can overflow and actually cause floods.
The farmland downstream no longer gets the fresh silt that used to fertilise it. Fish also cannot swim upstream to lay eggs because the dam blocks them.
Thousands of people lose their homes and jobs when big dams flood their villages. States also fight over how much river water each one gets.
Big dams have many problems.
Dams cause floods.
Building dams does not change how a river flows or how much sediment it carries; dams only store water.
Damming rivers has no effect on their natural flow. The only problem with dams is that they cause earthquakes.
